summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors.

Every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Negeri Sembilan is exposed to the Penal Code rather than to the Sharia layer.

Negeri Sembilan is the state whose cross-dressing offence was struck down on the record. In November 2014 Malaysia's Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992, which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution.

The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan because state legislatures lack criminal-law power, which leaves federal criminalisation of same-sex conduct fully intact. A crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment has been documented nationwide since the 2018 election.

Exposure for visitors concentrates in raids and venues rather than in private conduct. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 31 foreign nationals were among those held until their embassies intervened. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, and a further sauna raid followed in Penang within days. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing.

State-sponsored discrimination is recorded in a Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters report of 10 August 2022, drawn from interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Negeri Sembilan. The report states that every state and the federal territories have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct.
tangentialFactors:
The 2014 ruling in Negeri Sembilan is an outlier rather than the national position. Enforcement of the cross-dressing enactments sits with state Islamic religious departments, and none of those laws contains a legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Three states additionally bar women from posing as men.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and a constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014. The Federal Court's subsequent federalism rulings in Selangor and Kelantan left Penal Code offences untouched.

Official hostility is documented alongside the litigation. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out enforcement against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

Reform prospects are foreclosed by Islamist opposition, and on 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the relevant Penal Code provisions rather than repealing them.
localsOnly:
Malaysian citizens who are Muslim carry the Sharia layer as well as the Penal Code, and state religious departments enforce it locally. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed cross-dressing or gender-nonconformity enactments.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. Islamist rhetoric and state programs frame gender nonconformity as a matter for correction rather than protection.

There is no same-sex marriage and no general anti-discrimination law at federal or state level. A Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters report calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon "rehabilitation" programs and the rhetoric surrounding them.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state whether the November 2014 Court of Appeal declaration on section 66 remains operative today, nor whether Negeri Sembilan has since re-enacted, amended or left the provision in place. That question is unresolved on the sources provided.

No state-level enforcement figures for Negeri Sembilan appear in the inventory; the documented raid activity, including the Chow Kit operation of 28 November 2025 and the subsequent Penang raid, is recorded at federal-territory and other-state level.

Nothing in the inventory addresses entry screening, visa conditions, gender markers on identity documents, or access to healthcare for visitors, so no finding is offered on those points. The Human Rights Watch country profile relied on here was last updated 16 December 2025.
